analogy.p: A d.c. supply is like a conveyor belt moving in one direction at a steady speed: everything on it, like charge, is carried the same way all the time. An a.c. supply is like pushing and pulling a child on a swing: the push changes direction regularly, and 50 Hz means 50 complete back-and-forth movements every second. Just as the child's body only moves a small distance to and fro but the energy still gets passed along, the electrons in an a.c. wire only vibrate backwards and forwards but the energy is still transferred. The analogy breaks down because the swing's motion is set by gravity and the child's natural frequency, whereas the a.c. frequency is fixed by the generator at 50 Hz.
analogy.t: Pushing a child on a swing versus a conveyor belt

bullets: A p.d. is needed to make a **current** flow; current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
The direction of current in a circuit is decided by the direction of the p.d. across it: reverse the p.d. and the current reverses too.
**Direct p.d. (d.c.)** pushes charge in one direction only.
**Alternating p.d. (a.c.)** reverses direction repeatedly, so the current repeatedly reverses too.
A cell or battery provides d.c.; the mains socket provides a.c.
Both types can transfer energy to an appliance, which is why many devices (heaters, lamps) work on either.
Link to other topics: potential difference and energy, the National Grid (transformers need a.c.), and mains-plug safety.
core.h: What is a potential difference, and why does its type matter?
core.p: A **potential difference (p.d.)** is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V). It is the 'push' that drives charge round a circuit. The type of p.d. is decided by how that push behaves over time: either it stays the same way round all the time (**direct**), or it keeps swapping its direction (**alternating**). Knowing which type a source provides tells you how the current in the circuit behaves, which components can be used with it, and why different sources are used for different jobs.

bullets: A cell is typically 1.5 V; a car battery is typically 12 V.
On a p.d.-time graph a steady d.c. supply is a **flat horizontal line** that stays on one side of zero.
The positive terminal is drawn as the **longer line** in the cell symbol; conventional current leaves the positive terminal.
Other d.c. sources include solar cells (photovoltaic) and the output of a USB charger or a laptop power adapter.
Electronic components such as microprocessors, LEDs and many circuits need d.c. to work properly.
A **diode** only allows current in one direction, so it can be used with other components to convert a.c. into d.c. (this process is called rectification).
d.c. does not reverse, so a d.c. current used in a wire does not need to be reversed at any time; electrons drift steadily one way (opposite to conventional current).
core.p: With a **direct p.d.** the terminals of the supply keep the same polarity all the time, so the push on charge is always the same way round. This means the current flows in **one direction only** round the circuit. Cells and batteries produce a direct p.d. because chemical reactions inside them keep one terminal positive and the other negative. The size of the p.d. may stay constant (a fresh cell gives about 1.5 V) or it can change in size slowly as the cell runs down, but its direction never changes.

bullets: a.c. is produced by **generators (alternators)** in power stations, in which a coil and magnet rotate relative to each other.
The wave shape of mains is a **sine wave**.
A negative p.d. on the graph does not mean 'less energy'; it means the **direction** of the push is reversed.
In a wire carrying a.c. the free electrons do not travel round the circuit; they **vibrate back and forth** about fixed positions, but energy is still transferred.
A lamp lights and a heater warms up whichever way the current flows, so they work on a.c. or d.c.
Appliances needing d.c. (phone chargers, laptop adapters) contain a circuit that converts the a.c. mains to d.c. at a low p.d.
a.c. is used for the National Grid because its p.d. can be easily stepped up or down with transformers, which only work with a changing (alternating) p.d.
core.p: With an **alternating p.d.** the polarity of the supply keeps swapping. First one terminal is positive, then a fraction of a second later it is negative, and this repeats continuously. The current is therefore pushed one way round the circuit, slows to zero, then is pushed the other way round, and so on. Because the p.d. is continually changing in size as well as direction, an a.c. graph is a wave that rises above zero, falls through zero, goes below zero (meaning reversed direction) and then returns, repeating the same pattern over and over.

bullets: **Mains p.d. = about 230 V** (volts); never 230 A or 230 W: always give the correct unit.
**Mains frequency = 50 Hz**; one hertz (1 Hz) is one cycle per second.
Period of mains: T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = **0.02 s (20 ms)**.
In each cycle the current flows one way, then the other way, so there are **100 reversals of direction every second**.
This is much larger than a cell (1.5 V), which is why mains is so dangerous and why fuses and earthing are needed.
Other countries use different values; for example the USA uses about 120 V and 60 Hz, but you only need to know the UK values.
The mains p.d. is the p.d. between the **live** wire and the **neutral** wire, and also between live and earth.
core.p: You must recall the two numbers for UK mains electricity: the **p.d. is about 230 V** and the **frequency is 50 Hz**. Mains is an alternating supply. The 230 V is the effective value of the p.d.; the true peak p.d. is higher (about 325 V, see the Higher/extension section) but the specification and the mark scheme only ask for 230 V. A frequency of 50 Hz means the supply completes 50 full cycles every second, so each cycle lasts 1/50 s = 0.020 s.

bullets: **Frequency (Hz) = 1 / time period (s)**, written f = 1/T.
**Time period (s) = 1 / frequency (Hz)**, written T = 1/f.
One complete cycle goes from a point on the wave to the next identical point (for example peak to the next peak).
Example: a 100 Hz supply has T = 1/100 = 0.01 s = 10 ms.
Example: a supply with a period of 0.04 s has f = 1/0.04 = 25 Hz.
Convert units before calculating: 1 ms = 0.001 s; 20 ms = 0.020 s; 1 kHz = 1000 Hz.
Doubling the frequency halves the period.
Mains at 50 Hz is fast enough that a filament lamp does not visibly flicker, because the filament does not cool significantly between cycles.
core.h: Frequency and time period of an alternating supply
core.p: The **frequency** of an a.c. supply is the number of complete cycles it makes each second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. The **time period** is the time taken for one complete cycle, measured in seconds (s). They are linked by the equation f = 1 / T, which rearranges to T = 1 / f. A high frequency means a short period and a low frequency means a long period. These ideas are shared with the waves topic (4.6), so the same equation and units are used.

bullets: **Direction:** d.c. = one direction only; a.c. = direction reverses repeatedly.
**Source:** d.c. = cell, battery, solar cell; a.c. = mains from generators in power stations.
**Graph on an oscilloscope:** d.c. = flat horizontal line (not on zero); a.c. = wave that goes above and below zero.
**Size:** d.c. from a cell is steady; a.c. continually changes in size between zero and a maximum.
**Frequency:** d.c. has no frequency (it does not repeat a cycle); UK mains a.c. has a frequency of 50 Hz.
**Typical uses:** d.c. powers portable and electronic devices; a.c. is used for the National Grid, homes and large appliances.
**Transformers:** will only work with a.c., not steady d.c.
Both can heat a resistor and light a filament lamp; the energy transferred depends on the current, the p.d. and the time.
core.h: Comparing d.c. and a.c. (the key table of differences)
core.p: Examiners often ask you to compare the two types directly, so build a point-by-point comparison. The central contrast is direction: d.c. goes one way only, a.c. reverses. Next come the typical sources, the shape of the graph, and typical uses. Remember to compare like with like, for example 'a.c. reverses direction **but** d.c. does not' rather than listing facts about one only.

bullets: **Step 1:** find the length of one complete cycle in horizontal divisions (peak to peak).
**Step 2:** time period T = number of divisions x time base (convert ms into s).
**Step 3:** frequency f = 1 / T.
**Peak p.d.** = number of divisions from the centre line to the top of a peak x volts per division.
If the wave looks taller, the p.d. is greater; if the waves are squashed closer together, the frequency is higher.
A flat line above the centre line means d.c.; the height of that line gives the d.c. p.d.
If a trace shows more cycles across the screen with the same time base, the frequency is higher.
Always state the unit and show the working: method marks are given even if the final number is wrong.
core.h: Reading a p.d.-time graph and an oscilloscope trace
core.p: An **oscilloscope** displays how a p.d. varies with time. The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is p.d. The screen is divided by grid lines into **divisions**. The **time base** setting tells you how much time each horizontal division represents (for example 5 ms per division) and the **volts per division** setting tells you how much p.d. each vertical division represents. To analyse a trace you read the number of divisions, then multiply by the setting. A d.c. source gives a straight horizontal line displaced from the centre; an a.c. source gives a repeating wave centred on zero.

bullets: The **p.d. is the cause**; the **current is the effect**.
Electrons are negatively charged so they move towards the positive terminal; when the terminal polarity swaps, they reverse.
Conventional current is defined from positive to negative, opposite to electron flow.
In a.c. each electron moves only a tiny distance to and fro, but the energy is carried along the wire by the changing electric field (energy is transferred, not electrons travelling all the way).
This is why a.c. and d.c. can both heat a wire: the electrons still collide with the ions and transfer energy as thermal energy.
If asked 'what happens to the current if the p.d. is reversed?' answer: it flows in the opposite direction.
core.h: Worked reasoning: why does the current reverse?
core.p: To explain why a.c. current reverses, link cause and effect step by step, because mark schemes reward the chain of reasoning. In an a.c. supply the terminals alternately become positive and negative. When the p.d. is positive in one direction, free (conduction) electrons in the wire are pushed one way. When the p.d. reverses, the force on the electrons reverses and they are pushed back the other way. Since the electrons are charged particles and current is the flow of charge, the current direction therefore reverses with the p.d.

bullets: Generators in power stations produce a.c. directly as a coil rotates in a magnetic field.
Transformers need a **changing** magnetic field, which a.c. provides; steady d.c. gives no changing field and so no transformer action.
Stepping up the p.d. reduces the current, which reduces energy lost as heat in the cables (P = I squared R).
Cells and batteries are portable and do not need to be connected to a power station.
Many devices need d.c. internally, so adapters contain transformers and rectifiers to convert 230 V a.c. to a few volts d.c.
Link to the National Grid topic where this is developed in detail.
core.h: Why mains uses a.c. and cells use d.c.
core.p: Different sources suit different jobs. Mains is generated in huge power stations by rotating generators, which naturally produce an alternating p.d. Mains is also transmitted over long distances using the National Grid, where **transformers** step the p.d. up to very high values (to reduce energy wasted as heat) and then down again for homes; transformers work only with alternating p.d., so a.c. is used. Cells, by contrast, store energy chemically and can only provide a steady one-way p.d., which is ideal for portable, low-voltage electronics.

bullets: The peak is reached twice per cycle (once positive, once negative).
Because the peak is much more than 230 V, the instantaneous p.d. can be hazardous even though the quoted value is 230 V.
At exactly the moments the wave crosses zero, the p.d. is momentarily 0 V, but this lasts only a tiny fraction of a cycle.
For GCSE you only need to quote 'about 230 V' and 50 Hz.
If a question shows a graph with a peak of about 325 V, you can say this is consistent with the 230 V effective value.
core.h: Higher tier / extension: peak value and the meaning of 230 V
core.p: The 230 V quoted for mains is not the maximum height of the wave. Because the p.d. is continually changing, a single 'average' number is awkward (the true average of a sine wave over a cycle is zero). The figure 230 V is the **effective (root mean square, r.m.s.) value**: the steady d.c. p.d. that would transfer the same energy to a resistor. The peak value is the r.m.s. multiplied by the square root of 2 (about 1.41), giving roughly 325 V. This is beyond what is asked in the AQA specification wording, but helps explain why mains is so dangerous.

bullets: **Plug wiring and safety:** the live wire alternates between positive and negative p.d. relative to earth at 50 Hz; neutral stays near 0 V.
**Power and energy:** P = V I and E = P t use the supply p.d., for example a 230 V kettle.
**National Grid:** step-up and step-down transformers work only with a.c.
**Electromagnetism (4.7):** generators and transformers use changing magnetic fields.
**Waves (4.6):** f = 1/T and the idea of a wave cycle apply to a.c.
**Required practical on resistance and I-V characteristics:** these use d.c. supplies; a.c. would make the readings change constantly.
core.p: This small topic connects to several big ideas, and exam questions often combine them. Mains plug wiring and the National Grid depend on a.c. Power and energy calculations use the p.d. of the supply. The frequency equation links to waves. Understanding these links lets you tackle multi-step questions confidently.

bullets: 'State the frequency and p.d. of UK mains' - **50 Hz and about 230 V**.
'Explain the difference between a.c. and d.c.' - 'a.c. **changes direction** repeatedly, whereas d.c. flows in **one direction** only'.
'What does the oscilloscope trace show?' - a wave above and below zero shows a.c.; a flat line shows d.c.
Always include units; 230 V not 230.
If asked for the number of reversals per second, double the frequency: 100.
Show the equation f = 1/T before substituting.
Use 'potential difference' (not 'voltage') in your answers where possible, as this is the AQA wording.
core.h: How to answer typical question styles
core.p: Questions on this topic are usually short recall or interpretation marks, and they are easily lost through imprecise wording. Learn the exact phrases. For 'state' questions give the value with its unit. For 'describe the difference' questions write a comparative sentence using the word 'whereas' or 'but'. For graph questions say what the trace looks like and what it means, then use numbers if given.

exam: **1 mark (state):** 'Mains is a.c. with a p.d. of about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz' - always include both numbers and units.
**1-2 marks (difference):** 'd.c. flows in one direction only whereas a.c. continually changes direction' - use a comparative word such as 'whereas'.
**2 marks (oscilloscope):** one mark for identifying the trace (flat line = d.c.; wave above and below zero = a.c.) and one for the reason (direction does or does not change).
**Calculation (3 marks):** write f = 1/T (1 mark), substitute with the time period converted to seconds (1 mark), answer with the unit Hz (1 mark).
**Reading divisions:** period = number of divisions for one cycle x time base; check the time base units (ms or s) before calculating.
**Command word 'explain':** give the reason - for example 'the current reverses **because** the p.d. reverses'.
**Command word 'compare':** write both sides in the same sentence and make a direct comparison.
**Number of reversals:** 50 Hz gives 100 changes of direction per second (twice the frequency); a common 1-mark extension.
**Graph tip:** if a trace has the same height but more waves across the screen the frequency is higher; if the waves are taller the p.d. is larger.
**Link marks:** in 6-mark questions on the National Grid, mention that a.c. is needed so that transformers can change the p.d.

mistakes.r: Mains is a potential difference of about 230 V. Give the correct unit.
mistakes.w: The mains supply is 230 A (or 230 W).

mistakes.r: a.c. means the direction of the p.d. and current reverses repeatedly.
mistakes.w: a.c. means the voltage changes in size only.

mistakes.r: d.c. means the current flows in one direction only; its size may still change.
mistakes.w: d.c. means the current stays the same size.

mistakes.r: The frequency is 50 Hz, which means 50 cycles per second; do not add 'per second' to Hz.
mistakes.w: Mains has a frequency of 50 (no unit) or 50 Hertz per second.

mistakes.r: In a.c. the electrons vibrate back and forth; energy is transferred along the wire.
mistakes.w: Electrons travel all the way from the power station to my house in a.c.
The time period of 50 Hz is 50 s.

mistakes.r: Negative means the direction of the p.d. is reversed; energy is still transferred.
mistakes.w: A negative p.d. on an a.c. graph means no energy is supplied.

mistakes.r: Potential difference (V) is the push; current (A) is the flow of charge. Keep them separate.
mistakes.w: Using the word 'voltage' and 'current' as if they were the same.

mistakes.r: Period is read along the horizontal (time) axis for one full cycle, then multiplied by the time base.
mistakes.w: Reading the oscilloscope time period from the peak height.

summary: The specification asks you to know that the mains supply in the UK is an alternating potential difference (a.c.) of about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz, and to explain the difference between direct potential difference (d.c.) and alternating potential difference. It matters because it underpins every mains-safety, National Grid and transformer question in Paper 1, and because oscilloscope-trace and frequency calculations are easy marks if you know the routine.

terms.d: The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts (V). It is the push that makes charge flow.
The rate of flow of electric charge; measured in amperes (A).
A p.d. that always pushes charge in the same direction, so that the current flows in one direction only; supplied by cells and batteries.
A p.d. that repeatedly reverses direction, so that the current repeatedly changes direction; supplied by the mains.
The number of complete cycles of a wave or alternating supply in one second; measured in hertz (Hz).
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
The time taken for one complete cycle; measured in seconds (s); T = 1 / f.
One complete repeat of an alternating pattern, from one point on the wave to the next identical point.
The electricity supplied to homes in the UK: an a.c. supply of about 230 V at a frequency of 50 Hz.
A device that displays how a p.d. varies with time as a trace on a grid; used to show d.c. and a.c. supplies.
The oscilloscope setting that gives the time represented by each horizontal division (for example 5 ms per division).
A device in which a coil and magnet move relative to each other to produce an alternating p.d.
A device that changes the size of an alternating p.d. using a changing magnetic field; it does not work with steady d.c.
A component that only allows current to flow in one direction; used to convert a.c. into d.c.

worked.q: An oscilloscope trace of the mains supply shows one complete cycle across 4 horizontal divisions. The time base is set to 5 ms per division. Calculate the frequency of the supply. (3 marks)
steps: Time for one cycle: T = 4 divisions x 5 ms = 20 ms.

worked.q: A signal generator is set to a frequency of 250 Hz. Calculate the time period of the signal in milliseconds. (3 marks)

worked.ans: d.c. gives current in one direction only, e.g. from a battery; a.c. repeatedly reverses direction, e.g. the 230 V, 50 Hz mains.
worked.q: Explain the difference between direct and alternating potential difference and give one source of each. (4 marks)
steps: Direct p.d.: the current flows in one direction only (1 mark).
Alternating p.d.: the direction of the p.d. and current reverses repeatedly (1 mark).
Source of d.c.: a cell or battery (1 mark).
